Tuesday, 8 June 2032. The local radio station in Grenoble is holding a debate about the new music hall in the former glove factory. Face to face: Mrs Faure, an opposition town councillor, and Julien. A journalist moderates.
Good evening, everyone. Tonight we’re talking about the future music hall in the former glove factory. Mrs Faure, you have the floor.
Thank you. I want to say this straight away: I’m not against culture. However, I doubt this hall is a priority for our neighbourhood.
Let me finish, please. Our schools need work done. Now, people would rather have a concert hall built.
I grant you, schools are important. But it isn’t a concert hall. It’s a rehearsal room for the children of the nearby school.
Granted. The fact remains that local residents were not consulted.
There I disagree. We had a letter delivered to every resident in March.
A letter isn’t enough. It seems to me we need a real debate, in public.
You’re not wrong. That’s why I suggest showing the site to everyone who wants to see it, and coming to Friday’s public meeting.
There’s a concrete proposal. Mrs Faure, what do you think?
I don’t think that’s enough. Nevertheless, I won’t oppose it.
Thank you. I’m not asking you to be convinced. I’m only asking you to come and see.

I grant you, schools are important. But…

Le premier vol de la grand-mère

At the beginning of June, a little yellow leaflet appeared in every letterbox in the old glove factory’s neighbourhood in Grenoble. It announced a public meeting on Friday 11 June at six p.m. in the function hall. The topic was written in capital letters: “A music hall in our neighbourhood: for or against?” Underneath, someone had added by hand: “Come in large numbers.”

Joseph, the head carpenter, brought the leaflet to Julien one morning on the site. He had found it in his daughter’s letterbox. “It’s the residents of rue des Tanneurs,” he explained. “They’re afraid of the noise, the cars, the children. And there’s a town councillor egging them on. Mrs Faure. She’s against anything that costs money. Especially when it wasn’t her idea.”

Julien read the leaflet twice. Then he called Amina, who opened a spreadsheet titled “Grenoble meeting”. Then he called Inès. Inès was in the middle of revising for her end-of-school exam, surrounded by geography cards, but she took the time to listen. At the end, she gave him just one piece of advice: “Don’t speak first. Let them speak. Listen to what they’re really afraid of losing. Then answer that, and only that.”

On Friday 11 June, the function hall was full. There were at least two hundred people sitting on plastic chairs under buzzing neon lights. In the front row, the residents of rue des Tanneurs, arms folded. On the platform, a table, four microphones, a jug of water. The mayor, who was chairing the meeting, looked like someone who would rather have been elsewhere.

Mrs Faure spoke first. She was a woman of about sixty, very elegant, with a voice used to microphones. She spoke for a quarter of an hour. She said she wasn’t against culture, of course. But she doubted this hall was a priority. The city had schools to renovate and roads to resurface. And she didn’t think the residents had been consulted enough.

Then the residents spoke, one after another. An elderly man was afraid of noise in the evening. A young mother was afraid the parents’ cars would block the street. A shopkeeper feared his parking spaces would be taken away. Finally, an old lady said in a small voice that she had lived opposite the factory for fifty-two years, and didn’t want anyone to transform it.

Julien wrote everything down. He interrupted no one. He let a whole hour go by without saying a word, which greatly surprised Mrs Faure, who had expected a fight. When the mayor finally gave him the floor, he stood up, took the microphone, and turned not to Mrs Faure, but to the old lady in the front row.

“Madam,” he said, “you said you have lived opposite the factory for fifty-two years. So you knew the women who worked there.” The old lady nodded. Her name was Mrs Rey. She had worked at the factory herself, from 1968 to 1995. She sewed leather gloves by hand, on the second floor, by the big window. She had known the factory full, then the factory empty.

“Then you know better than I do what an empty building is,” said Julien. “I’m not asking you to like our project. I’m only asking you to come and see before anything is decided. Monday, at five p.m. I’ll show you round myself. And if, after the visit, you still think it’s a bad idea, I promise to tell the mayor.” The room fell silent.

Then he answered the others, one by one, using exactly their own words. The noise? Radu had planned soundproofing; besides, rehearsals would stop at seven p.m. The cars? The children would come on foot from the nearby school. Parking? Nobody would touch a single space. He had brought the plans. He had them passed from row to row.

Mrs Faure took the microphone again. “All this is very nice, Mr Moreau,” she said. “Admittedly, you speak well. However, I’m not sure the residents need an orchestra. They need roads.” There was some applause. Julien smiled. He had expected this argument. He was about to reply when someone at the back of the hall started drumming.

It was a nine-year-old boy with two pencils in his hands, drumming on the back of the chair in front of him. A fast, regular, complicated rhythm that made the plastic vibrate. His mother tried to make him stop. He didn’t stop. Joseph, sitting next to him, put his hand on his daughter’s shoulder. “Let him be,” he said. “That’s Mathis. My grandson.”

The whole room had turned round. Mathis, who hadn’t noticed, kept drumming, eyes closed, as if he were alone in the world. Then he opened his eyes, saw two hundred people looking at him, and went bright red. He put down his pencils. In the silence, Joseph stood up, slowly, with his big carpenter’s hands.

“Mrs Faure,” he said, “I’ve known you a long time. I redid the roof frame of your house in 2015. I respect you. But my grandson has been drumming on every table since he could hold a pencil. At school, he gets punished. At home, he’s told to be quiet. Nobody has ever given him a drum kit. So, your roads, fine. But he needs a door.”

He sat down again. Nobody applauded. It wasn’t the kind of thing you applaud. But something had changed in the room. The shopkeeper unfolded his arms. The young mother leaned towards her neighbour to whisper something in her ear. And Mrs Faure, for the first time that evening, didn’t take the microphone again.

On Monday 14 June, at five p.m., Mrs Rey came to the factory. She walked slowly, with a cane, and often stopped to catch her breath. Julien was waiting for her at the door. He offered her his arm. She politely refused. She knew the way. She had walked it every morning for twenty-seven years.

The roof was almost finished. Joseph’s carpenters had laid the last oak beams the week before, and in the middle of the roof, exactly where there had been a hole, a huge window now let in the June light. Mrs Rey stopped in the middle of the factory, under the window. She looked up. For a long time she said nothing.

Then she pointed to a spot on the wall, near one of the big second-floor windows. “That was my place,” she said. “There. I sewed gloves for hands I would never see. The hands of rich ladies, in Paris, in New York.” She turned to Julien. “And now there will be children making music with their hands, here, in my place.”

She asked whether she could come and listen to the rehearsals. Julien answered that a chair would be kept for her in the front row, by the window, in her place. Mrs Rey nodded. The next day, the mayor received a handwritten letter on lined paper, signed by Mrs Rey and twenty-three residents of rue des Tanneurs. The letter was three lines long. It simply said: “We are for it.”

Mrs Faure, for her part, said nothing in public. But the following Saturday, Joseph saw her arrive at the site, alone, unannounced, with an umbrella and town shoes. She walked round the factory in silence. She looked at the roof, the oak beams, the big window. Then, before leaving, she left a note for Julien, folded in two on a crate: “I won’t oppose it. Provided the roof holds.” Joseph laughed for a week.

Meanwhile, in Lyon, Inès was sitting her end-of-school exam. The written papers took place on 28 and 29 June. She had revised until two in the morning every night, at the kitchen table, while her mother worked at the hospital. On the morning of the first paper, her mother had come home from her night shift just in time to make her breakfast and walk her to the school gate.

The French essay asked pupils to describe “a moment when you understood something important about other people”. Inès looked at the sheet for five minutes without writing. Then she smiled and wrote the story of a four-year-old girl who calmed a baby with a harmonica. She didn’t use any names. She only wrote, at the end: “Silence is also a way of talking to others.”

The results came out on 9 July, posted on the school railings. Inès didn’t want to go alone. She went with her mother, Théo, Claire, Yanis, Sami, and a dozen children from the orchestra who had insisted on coming. She looked for her name on the list, her finger trembling. Then she read, next to it: “Passed. With highest honours.”

Her mother screamed so loudly the whole neighbourhood heard her. Then she cried. Then she hugged everyone, including the school caretaker, who hadn’t asked for anything. Claire, for her part, had other news. Inès had been accepted at the Croix-Rousse lycée, in the music section, with an adapted timetable so she could attend Conservatoire classes at the same time.

“You’re going to have to work even harder,” Claire warned her. “I doubt you’ll have much holiday for three years.” Inès replied that she had never had holidays anyway, so it wouldn’t change much. Then she asked whether she could keep playing in the La Duchère orchestra. Claire said it was actually a condition.

One big event remained before the summer: little Yves’s christening. Lucia and Radu had chosen Sunday 18 July, at the Romanian Orthodox parish in Lyon, a little church hidden in a street in the 7th arrondissement. The priest, Father Vasile, had come from Suceava fifteen years earlier. He spoke French with such a strong accent that even Romanians sometimes struggled to understand him.

There was a problem. The godfather, Yves Le Goff, was Catholic, Breton, and hadn’t set foot in a church since his wife’s funeral in 2009. Father Vasile received him in his office a week before to discuss it. The conversation lasted two hours. Nobody ever found out exactly what they said to each other. But at the end they came out together laughing, and the priest said there was no problem at all.

The other problem was Grandma. She was eighty-six, the doctor had forbidden her the coach, and she had declared she would not miss her great-grandson’s christening, even if she had to walk. Dan had found the only possible solution. He had bought her a plane ticket, Iași–Lyon, with a connection in Munich. She had never flown in her life.

She refused for three days. She said that if God had wanted people to fly, he would have given them wings. Dan pointed out that God hadn’t given her wheels either, and yet she had crossed Europe by coach about ten times. Grandma thought about this argument for a long time. Then she said she would let herself be persuaded, but she would take her icon.

On Thursday 15 July, at Iași airport, the whole street had come to see her off. The neighbours had made sandwiches, pickled gherkins and a bottle of holy water. Security confiscated the holy water and the bread knife she had slipped into her bag “just in case”. Grandma argued with the officer for ten minutes, in Romanian, in front of a queue of laughing passengers.

On the plane, she refused to sit by the window. Then, once in the air, she demanded to be allowed to change seats so she could look. Dan spent the whole flight negotiating with the flight attendants. In Munich, she found the airport too big, too clean and too quiet. She asked Dan whether Germans ever talked. Dan said yes, but not at the airport.

The second flight, from Munich to Lyon, passed over the Alps. It was a perfectly clear day. Grandma pressed her forehead against the window and didn’t say a word for an hour. Below the plane, the mountains rolled past, white and blue, with their glaciers, their lakes, their deep valleys. When Dan asked if she was all right, she replied that she was talking with God and should be left in peace.

At Lyon airport, the whole family was waiting behind the barrier. Ioana had made a sign with Rose-Hélène: “Welcome, Bunica!”, with a plane drawn in felt-tip and a smiling sun. Grandma came out last, on Dan’s arm, in her Sunday headscarf, her icon clutched to her chest. She saw the sign. She saw Rose-Hélène. And she said: “The world is small, seen from above.”

Rose-Hélène asked her whether she had seen Odile up there in the sky. Grandma thought very seriously. Then she replied that she hadn’t seen her, but that while passing over the mountains, she had heard someone whistling. Rose-Hélène nodded, very satisfied. It was exactly the answer she had been waiting for.

The day before the christening, Grandma wanted to see the baby before anyone else. She had herself driven to Radu and Lucia’s first thing on Saturday morning. She took little Yves in her arms, examined him from head to toe, counted his fingers, then declared that he had the ears of his great-grandfather Ion, Lucia’s chin, and the character of someone she didn’t know yet.

“He has his godfather’s character,” said Lucia. “You’ll meet him tomorrow.” Grandma asked what this godfather did. Lucia said he had been a sailor for fifty years. Grandma pulled a face. In her family, she said, nobody had ever trusted sailors, because they always left. Lucia smiled. “This one,” she replied, “always comes back.”

On Sunday 18 July, the little church was packed. There were Lyon’s Romanians, who had come with their families, the women in headscarves, the men in white shirts. There were the French members of the family, a little lost, not knowing when to stand up or when to cross themselves. There were Isabelle, Théo, Claire, Amina, Inès and her mother. And there was Yves Le Goff, in a navy-blue suit and tie, more nervous than before a storm.

The ceremony lasted an hour and a half. Father Vasile chanted in Romanian, then repeated certain sentences in French for the guests, with his incredible accent. The church smelled of incense and wax. The icons gleamed in the candlelight. Yves held the baby in his arms with the same care as at the hospital, like a sea chart that must on no account be creased.

Then came the most impressive moment for the French: the immersion. The priest took the baby from Yves’s arms, undressed him completely and plunged him three times into the big font, all the way, head included. Isabelle let out a little cry. Mrs Roux, who had come in her wheelchair, made the Catholic sign of the cross, then the Orthodox one, so as not to upset anyone.

Little Yves, for his part, howled. An enormous, furious, magnificent cry that echoed under the vault of the little church. Father Vasile laughed. He said in Romanian, then in French, that children who cry at their christening have good lungs and a long life. Yves Le Goff replied, very seriously, that with lungs like that, the little one would make an excellent sailor. The whole church laughed.

But the baby went on howling. They put his white clothes back on, gave him back to his godfather, and he was still howling. Lucia came closer. So did Radu. Father Vasile waited patiently, his book in his hand. Then, from the front row, a four-year-old girl stood up without asking anyone’s permission. She took a harmonica out of the pocket of her Sunday dress.

Ioana tried to hold her back. Julien gently took her arm. “Let her,” he murmured. Rose-Hélène walked up to her godfather-by-heart and her cousin, in the middle of the church, in front of the gilded iconostasis. She played the three notes. In the church, nobody moved any more. Then she whistled the next three. The baby fell silent.

Father Vasile looked at the little girl, then at the baby, then at Yves, who had tears in his eyes. He didn’t know the whole story. Part of it had been told to him a week earlier, in his office. He put his hand on Rose-Hélène’s head. Then he said, in his incredible French, something everyone understood: “There. Now he is truly baptised.”

After the ceremony there was a meal in the parish hall under the church. The Romanian women had made sarmale, plăcinte and a mountain of cozonac. Grandma, barely recovered from her journey, took charge of the kitchen in less than five minutes. Yves Le Goff took his cast-iron pan out of his bag. Nobody was surprised. He made galettes for a hundred and twenty people.

Grandma tasted a galette. She chewed for a long time, looking suspicious. Then she declared it was almost as good as Romanian clătite, and that for a Frenchman, it was remarkable. Yves replied that he wasn’t French, he was Breton. Grandma said she couldn’t see the difference. The discussion lasted two hours, in two languages, without either of them really understanding the other. They became friends.

Towards the end of the meal, Julien received a message from Radu, who had left for Grenoble an hour earlier with Lucia’s blessing and a box of sarmale. Joseph and his carpenters had worked all weekend to finish the roof before the holidays. The message contained only a photo. It showed the big hall of the old glove factory, empty, clean, with its brick walls.

In the middle of the hall, under the big window in the roof, a ray of sunlight fell diagonally on the concrete floor. And in that ray of sunlight there were three people. Joseph, with his big hands. Mrs Rey, on a chair, in her place, by the window. And Mathis, sitting on the floor in front of an old second-hand drum kit his grandfather had bought him, sticks raised, ready to begin.

Under the photo, Radu had written a single sentence: “The light gets through.” Julien showed the photo to Ioana, then to Lucia, then to Isabelle, then to Grandma, who asked what it was. Julien explained to her in Romanian, in his own words, still a little clumsy after six years of lessons. Grandma looked at the photo for a very long time. Then she crossed herself.

“It’s a church,” she said. “A church without a priest, but a church all the same.” Julien wanted to protest, to explain that it was a music hall, not a place of worship. Then he looked at the photo again, the ray of light, the old lady, the boy with his sticks. And he thought that Grandma might not be completely wrong.

That same evening, Joseph sent Julien a video. It showed Mathis playing for the first time under the big window, on his old drum kit. It was noisy, clumsy, far too fast. Mrs Rey, on her chair, was beating time with her cane. At the end, she applauded on her own, for a long time, in the empty hall. Mathis stood up and bowed, very seriously, as if at the Odéon.

That evening, on rue d’Austerlitz, everyone was exhausted. Grandma was sleeping in Isabelle’s guest room, on the other side of the landing, with her icon on the bedside table. Yves Le Goff was sleeping on Isabelle’s sofa, because Grandma had taken his bed and he hadn’t dared argue. Henri-Ion was asleep. Rose-Hélène was pretending to be asleep.

Julien and Ioana were sitting on the balcony in the July heat, with the lights of Fourvière in front of them. Ioana rested her head on Julien’s shoulder. She said that six years ago, when she had arrived in Lyon with a suitcase and a dictionary, she would never have believed her grandmother would one day fly in to christen a little Breton in a Romanian church.

Julien laughed. He corrected her: the baby wasn’t Breton, he was Franco-Romanian, and it was his godfather who was Breton. Ioana replied that in this family, anyway, nobody really knew any more who was what. And that this was perhaps, in the end, the best news of the year. Julien didn’t answer. He was thinking the same thing.

That was when they heard it. On the other side of the landing, through Isabelle’s door, someone was whistling. Off-key, very off-key, with lots of air. The first three notes of the waltz. It wasn’t Yves: Yves was snoring, you could hear him from here. Ioana sat up, astonished. It was Grandma. Grandma, who had never whistled in her life, because in Moldavia, she said, a woman who whistles attracts the devil.

There was a silence. Then, from Rose-Hélène’s room, a small voice that wasn’t asleep at all answered with the next three notes. Ioana put her hand over her mouth. Julien smiled in the dark. And on the balcony, above the sleeping city, he whistled in turn, very softly, the rest of the waltz, up to the silence. Eight bars. Then nothing. Only the July night, and the family, on each side of the landing, complete at last.

The day after the public meeting, the local newspaper publishes a report. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. Look for the subjunctive, the connectors and the faire/se voir constructions. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Usine de gants : les riverains changent d’avis
On Friday evening, more than two hundred people gathered in the function hall to debate the plan for a music hall in the former glove factory. The debate promised to be tense.

Mrs Faure, an opposition town councillor, opened the evening. She declared that she was not against culture, but that she doubted the project was a priority. Several residents then expressed their fears: noise, traffic, parking.

Julien Moreau, coordinator of the “Musique en partage” network, let everyone speak for an hour before replying. First, he had the plans passed round the hall. He then offered to show residents around the site.

The turning point of the evening came from a child. Mathis, nine, the site foreman’s grandson, began drumming an impressive rhythm on a chair. His grandfather then took the floor to explain that the boy, often punished at school, had never had an instrument.
On Monday, after a visit to the site, Mrs Rey, a former factory worker, sent the mayor a letter signed by twenty-three residents. It fits into three words: “We are for it.”

Mrs Faure, for her part, was asked the question by our newspaper. Her answer: “I don’t think all the problems have been solved. Nevertheless, I acknowledge that this project makes sense.” The hall is expected to open in January 2033.

Letter to the local newspaper (DELF B2)

Write (at least 250 words) in French a letter to the “Courrier des lecteurs” section of a local newspaper, about a project in your town (a sports hall, a park, a cycle lane). Concede your opponents’ arguments, then defend your position. Use everything you have learnt in this unit.
I used at least one concession phrase (je vous l’accorde, admettons, certes… mais).
I used the subjunctive after “je ne pense pas que / je doute que”.
I used the indicative after “je suis convaincu que / il me semble que”.
I used at least one construction with faire or laisser + infinitive.
I ended with a concrete proposal.
Dear Sir or Madam, I would like to respond to your article on the planned cycle lane along the river.
Some residents doubt this project is useful. I grant that it will be expensive, and that some trees will have to be cut down.
The fact remains that traffic has become unbearable. Indeed, it takes forty minutes to cross the centre by car. Now, by bike, it would take fifteen.
I am convinced this cycle lane will change the lives of thousands of residents. On the other hand, I don’t think the town hall has consulted the shopkeepers enough.
Consequently, I propose that residents be allowed to vote on the route before work begins.
